feed.title: Henrik Sjöstrand
feed.subtitle: Notes on tools I build and use: the problems they address and the approaches they take.

entry.title: Introducing jix: separating dependency resolution from the Java build
entry.summary: jix resolves Maven dependencies once, pins them with Nix, and lets builds be written as ordinary code.
entry.content:
I am releasing jix, a tool that resolves Java dependencies from Maven Central, pins the complete graph and every artifact hash, and provides the result to Nix. The locked classpaths can be used with an existing build, or with jix's optional build DSL, in which a build is a few lines of ordinary code.

Why

Maven's dependency ecosystem deserves credit at the outset. Group/artifact/version coordinates, POMs that declare a library's requirements, and Maven Central, a single repository holding nearly every Java library with roughly twenty years of history, gave Java the strongest dependency ecosystem of its generation, and later package managers in other languages have drawn on it. jix does not replace any of this; it depends on it.

The difficulty lies elsewhere. A build often has a simple, well-understood goal: compile these sources against these JARs and include a given file in the resulting JAR. Achieving it in Maven may nonetheless require reading about resource inclusion, choosing among several plugins that each nearly fit, and investigating lifecycle phases. Because the build tool owns dependency resolution, it also owns every other step of the build.

Even when the build works, dependencies are resolved at build time, from the network, with whichever JDK is present. The same project can therefore produce different results on different days.

How it works

jix keeps the ecosystem and separates the two responsibilities. It performs the difficult part, resolving dependencies from Maven Central with Maven's semantics, including scopes, BOMs, and exclusions, and records the complete graph and every artifact hash in jix.lock. From that point on, dependencies are pinned Nix values, and the build is ordinary code.

Dependencies are declared with ordinary Maven coordinates. Here the application uses Guava:

jix lock resolves Guava together with its transitive dependencies (failureaccess, jspecify, and others) and writes the result to jix.lock. The build then refers to the locked classpaths as deps.classpaths.main and deps.classpaths.runtime.

Including a resource takes one line. The following is a complete executable JAR build:

Where the DSL is insufficient, deps.classpaths.main is a plain Nix derivation containing the pinned JARs. A custom build step can invoke javac with it directly, without a plugin API.

Design choice

Builds never resolve dependencies or update locks. A missing or stale jix.lock causes the build to fail rather than fall back to the network.

Features

  • Two lock files: flake.lock pins toolchains; jix.lock pins Maven selections, hashes, and resolution contexts.
  • Incremental adoption: locked classpaths can be used with an existing build first, and the build DSL adopted later or not at all.
  • Multiple environments: named Java/OS contexts are declared once, and jix lock pins all of them.
  • Plain Nix outputs: jix build jar is equivalent to nix build .#jar, so standard binary caches apply.
  • IDE support: jix idea generates IntelliJ configuration from the same pinned inputs.

Design

Build tools combine two different tasks: dependency resolution, which is difficult and must be exact, and building, which for the most part means running javac and packaging the result. Because the two are combined, the cost of the first is paid in the complexity of the second.

Maven solved the difficult part, and the Java ecosystem rests on that solution. jix reuses it rather than reimplementing it: resolution uses the same repositories and the same semantics, verified against Maven 3.9 and Resolver 1.9, and the result is provided as pinned, hash-checked inputs. How those inputs are used is left to the build author, in a language suited to describing builds.

Availability

jix is open source and available on GitHub. It runs on Linux (x86-64 and AArch64) and requires Nix. A new project with an executable JAR build is three commands away: jix init --template fat, jix lock, and jix run. Issues and feedback are welcome.

entry.title: Read-only agent access to a corporate Confluence
entry.summary: A small setup — confluence-cli, an agent skill, and SecretSpec — for retrieving and consolidating information from an internal wiki.
entry.content:
Background

Much of the information I need at work is held in Confluence. Retrieving it was, in practice, laborious: a search, followed by reading several pages side by side and assembling an answer manually.

Two properties of the material made this harder. First, a substantial share of it was outdated. Pages had been written years apart by different authors, and frequently described a state that no longer held, with no indication of which page was authoritative. Second, reference documentation was often divided across pages that linked to one another, where some links pointed to pages that had since moved and others were broken.

Each lookup therefore involved verifying the currency of every page and following every link. In many cases asking a colleague was the cheaper option.

Reading and comparing sources of this kind is work I already delegate to a coding agent when the sources are code. What was missing was access to the wiki.

Setup

The agent is given confluence-cli through a skill: a short instruction file that specifies which commands to use for searching, reading, and exporting pages, and which actions are prohibited.

Given a question, the agent searches the relevant space, traverses the page tree and the links between pages (searching for the new location where a page has moved), exports the relevant pages as Markdown, and reads them together. The output is a draft answer with references to its sources, together with a note of where sources disagree and which source was preferred.

I use this for two purposes:

  • Documents: consolidating material spread over many pages into a single text, which I then review, correct, and share.
  • Data: extracting the same attributes from many inconsistently structured pages into a table, with each value referenced to its source page.

In both cases my role shifts from retrieval to review. The results have, in my experience, been more complete than what I produced manually.

Design choice

The agent reads; publication remains manual. The CLI profile is read-only, and any write operation requires a plan to be reviewed before apply.

Credential handling

A read-only profile is insufficient if the agent has access to the personal access token, since any value in the agent's context may appear in logs, transcripts, or commands it constructs. The token is therefore kept outside the agent's context entirely, using SecretSpec.

The token remains in the pass password store, where it was already kept. A secretspec.toml alongside the skill declares the required secret and its location:

The skill requires every invocation to be wrapped as follows, with a stated reason:

secretspec run --file secretspec.toml --scope confluence-cli \
  --reason "User-requested Confluence task" -- \
  confluence --profile default search "some topic"

SecretSpec reads the token from pass and places it only in the environment of the single confluence process. The agent observes the command and its output but not the value. The scope restricts the wrapper to that one secret, and the skill prohibits direct retrieval (secretspec get, env, shell tracing).

A secondary effect was the removal of a duplicate credential: the CLI had stored its own copy of the token in a configuration file, which could be revoked once SecretSpec was in place. A single copy now exists, and each use of it is explicit.

Contributions

Two obstacles prevented this setup from working in my environment. I addressed both upstream, and both changes were merged:

  • System certificate trust: the CLI now uses the operating-system certificate store, and so works against a Confluence instance behind an internal certificate authority.
  • A Nix flake: the CLI can be pinned in a devenv, which makes a known version available to the agent.

Discussion

The setup requires few components: a CLI with predictable behaviour, a page of instructions, and SecretSpec to keep the credential out of reach. No integration platform or dedicated bot is involved. The relevant judgement is encoded in the skill file: narrow queries, page content treated as data rather than instructions, and no writes without explicit approval. These constraints are what made it acceptable, in my view, to give an agent access to the wiki at all.

entry.title: Introducing cryo: API regression tests from existing curl examples
entry.summary: cryo turns curl examples already present in a codebase, and OpenAPI operations, into reviewed HTTP snapshot tests.
entry.content:
I am releasing cryo, a tool for HTTP snapshot testing. It finds the curl examples already present in a codebase, or imports operations from an OpenAPI specification, records their responses as readable snapshots, and reports later changes for review.

Why

API regression tests are valuable but tedious to write, and are consequently often absent. At the same time, READMEs and code comments frequently contain working curl examples, and an OpenAPI specification, where one exists, already enumerates every operation.

How it works

cryo applies approval testing to HTTP APIs:

discover → bless → check → diff or fix → recheck → accept
  • Discover: locate localhost curl commands anywhere in the source tree, or import OpenAPI 3.0/3.1 operations.
  • Bless: record known-good responses as readable, canonical HTTP snapshots committed to the repository.
  • Check: on later runs, changed responses are recorded as candidates rather than overwriting the baseline.
  • Normalize: volatile values such as timestamps and identifiers are handled by explicit JSON/CSV replacement rules in the manifest, and are never accepted implicitly.

Environment variables for ports and credentials

Examples in documentation rarely hard-code a port or a credential, and cryo does not require them to. Environment variables in a discovered curl command become {{NAME}} placeholders in the manifest, and are read from the environment when check or bless runs. Consider an example in a README:

curl "http://localhost:$APP_PORT/api/status" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $API_TOKEN"

Discovery records it in .cryo/requests.http without resolving either variable:

### status-get
# @source README.md:42
# @enabled true
GET http://localhost:{{APP_PORT}}/api/status
Authorization: Bearer {{API_TOKEN}}

The same manifest therefore runs against a locally started application on whichever port it was given, or in CI with a token supplied by the pipeline, and no credential is committed. Basic authentication given with curl -u is recorded as # @basic-auth metadata instead.

export APP_PORT=8080
export API_TOKEN=$(pass dev/api-token)

cryo discover src test   # create or merge .cryo/requests.http
cryo bless               # record the initial snapshots

Removing fields that vary between runs

Snapshots retain only the status, Content-Type, and a canonical body. JSON is pretty-printed, volatile headers such as Date, Server, Set-Cookie, and Content-Length are discarded, and dynamic ports in absolute loopback links become {{PORT}}.

Values inside the body are a different matter, since cryo cannot know which of them are meaningful. A generated timestamp differs on every run, so the first check after bless reports the case as changed:

cryo check               # status-get: changed
cryo diff status-get     # the only difference is $.probes[*].generatedAt

cryo suggests a replacement command for each remaining scalar difference, but does not apply it. Once the field is confirmed to be genuinely nondeterministic, the rule is added explicitly:

cryo replace add status-get json '$.probes[*].generatedAt' '<generated-at>'
cryo recheck status-get
cryo accept status-get

The rule is stored with the request, so it is reviewed and versioned like the rest of the manifest:

### status-get
# @source README.md:42
# @enabled true
# @json-replace $.probes[*].generatedAt <generated-at>
GET http://localhost:{{APP_PORT}}/api/status
Authorization: Bearer {{API_TOKEN}}

CSV responses are handled in the same way, by column: cryo replace add report-get csv generated_at '<generated-at>'.

Design

cryo reuses tests that already exist instead of requiring new ones, and treats every change in a response as something to be reviewed. Defaults are conservative: discovery enables only side-effect-free loopback GET/HEAD requests, and OpenAPI import ignores the specification's servers field, so a production endpoint cannot become a test target by accident. Status changes are also classified; a transition from 200 to 500, for instance, is reported as a regression rather than as an ordinary difference.

Availability

cryo is open source and available on GitHub. Static Linux x86_64 archives, each with a SHA-256 checksum, are published under GitHub Releases. It can also be installed with cargo install --git https://github.com/hencjo/cryo cryo, which requires bash and curl on PATH, or run directly with nix run github:hencjo/cryo. Issues and feedback are welcome.

entry.title: Introducing Fransson: reproducible Kafka topics for local and test environments
entry.summary: Fransson is a one-directional tool for dumping, restoring, and cloning Kafka topics, with their partitioning and configuration intact.
entry.content:
I am releasing Fransson, a tool for reproducing Kafka topics in local and test environments. It dumps topics to archives and restores them, clones topics from a live cluster, and forwards new events, while keeping partitioning, topic configuration, and record contents intact.

Why

Development and testing against event-driven systems benefit from realistic data: the actual contents of compacted reference topics, actual message shapes, and actual volumes. Reproducing a Kafka topic faithfully in another cluster is, however, more involved than copying its records. The partition count and topic configuration must match, a live source must be copied without loss, and a dump must restore with the same result every time. Fransson was written to handle each of these explicitly.

How it works

Fransson is strictly one-directional: source connections are read-only, and all writes go to the configured destination. Each destination topic is declared with exactly one mode (clone, stream, restore, manage, or empty) together with the topic properties Fransson is to own:

Partition counts

A record's partition is determined by its key and the number of partitions, so a copy with a different count changes per-key ordering and breaks co-partitioning in consumers and Kafka Streams applications. Partition counts are therefore not configured for copied topics: clones and streams take them from the source, and restores from the archive. Every record is written to the partition it was read from, with key, payload, timestamp, and headers unchanged, and an existing destination with a different partition count is treated as drift.

Compaction and deletion settings

A topic's meaning depends on its configuration as much as on its records. A compacted reference topic restored with cleanup.policy=delete loses records once retention expires, and an event topic restored as compacted keeps only the latest record for each key. The properties listed under config are owned by Fransson, which also sets message.timestamp.type=CreateTime so that copied timestamps are retained; tombstones and zero-length records are copied as data.

Every destination is checked before anything is changed. A topic whose partition count or owned properties differ is recreated only with explicit --force, since recreation destroys its data. When a topic is created or recreated, committed consumer offsets for it are deleted, and an active consumer group on it causes the operation to fail.

Cloning live production data

A production topic keeps receiving writes while it is copied. A clone reads from the earliest offset and records its position only after the destination has acknowledged each write, revalidating source and destination topic identities before every checkpoint. If source retention removes records that have not yet been copied, the clone stops and requires --force to rebuild, rather than skipping ahead. A stream, by contrast, forwards only events produced while Fransson is running.

Dumps and snapshots

A dump reads every partition up to the high-watermark captured when the command starts, and fails if a captured offset expires during collection. Archives omit topic names and physical offsets, are written atomically, and identical partition contents produce byte-identical archives. Restores are recorded with the archive's SHA-256, so an applied archive is not applied again, and --only-if-empty restores only into topics proven empty by reading every partition.

fransson dump --config fransson.yaml \
  --source production:products --archive products.fransson.zst
fransson restore --config fransson.yaml --only-if-empty

Design

Fransson treats Kafka topics, including their shape and configuration, as something to be declared and reproduced, not only as a sequence of records to be copied. Risk is managed by restricting the design: a single direction of data flow, explicit modes, preflight checks before destructive operations, and a defined behaviour for restoring only into empty topics.

Availability

Fransson is open source and available on GitHub. It requires Kafka 2.8 or newer and can be run directly with nix run github:hencjo/fransson, or as a process in a devenv. Issues and feedback are welcome.

entry.title: Introducing stow: GitOps deployments for a single Docker host
entry.summary: stow is a GitOps reconciler for Docker service deployments, with changes reviewed as merge requests and automatic convergence on the host.
entry.content:
I am releasing stow, a small GitOps reconciler for service deployments on a Docker host. A GitLab repository holds the desired state, changes arrive as merge requests, and a daemon on the host converges the running containers to match, rolling back if a new instance fails verification.

Why

Not every service warrants Kubernetes, but reviewed, auditable, and repeatable deployments are desirable regardless of scale. On a single Docker host, deployment in practice tends to reduce to SSH sessions and shell scripts, with no record of who changed what, and no automatic way back when a release fails.

How it works

A GitLab repository is the source of truth. Each service is described by a stow.yaml descriptor and versioned configuration. A deployment proceeds as follows:

  1. The application pipeline builds and pushes an image.
  2. stow suggest-image opens or updates a merge request that pins the image digest, optionally with environment changes and a changelog. It neither merges nor deploys.
  3. After the merge, the deployment pipeline notifies the daemon on the host.
  4. stow daemon reconciles Docker with the latest commit on the default branch: it decrypts SOPS-managed configuration, computes a content hash, starts containers with matching labels, verifies the new instance, and rolls back automatically if verification fails.

Design

stow brings the principal properties of GitOps (declarative descriptors, digest-pinned artifacts, approval through merge requests, and observable convergence) to a single host, in one binary, without a cluster, operator, or control plane.

Several details are handled conservatively. YAML edits preserve unrelated content byte for byte, repeating a suggestion updates the existing merge request rather than creating a duplicate, and a target branch that has moved causes a safe failure rather than a race.

Availability

stow is open source and available on GitHub. It is a single binary, and requires a GitLab instance for the deployment repository and Docker on the host. Issues and feedback are welcome.

entry.title: Introducing Silo: a local OpenID Connect provider for development and testing
entry.summary: Silo is a local-only OpenID Connect mock provider, with a browser user picker and signed tokens, for development and tests.
entry.content:
I am releasing Silo, a local OpenID Connect provider for development and test environments. It runs the authorization-code flow in the browser with a built-in user picker, issues signed tokens, and publishes a JWKS endpoint, so applications can be run and tested locally without a corporate identity provider.

Why

Applications that authenticate through OpenID Connect are difficult to run locally. Using the production identity provider during development requires test accounts, network access, and registered redirect URLs, and makes switching between users cumbersome. Replacing the authentication code path with a development-only shortcut avoids those problems, but then the code under test is no longer the code that runs in production.

How it works

Silo implements the parts of an OpenID Connect provider that an application interacts with:

  • Endpoints: discovery at /Silo/.well-known/openid-configuration, together with authorization, token, and JWKS endpoints.
  • Tokens: RS256-signed ID and access tokens for the authorization-code flow. Refresh tokens are not issued.
  • User selection: a browser-based user picker in place of a login form, with mock users and their claims defined in YAML.
  • Client credentials: service-to-service tokens with scope-dependent mock claims.

Silo also works as a client. It can obtain access tokens on the command line, via authorization_code or client_credentials, from Silo itself or from a real issuer.

Design

Applications continue to validate genuine JWTs against a genuine JWKS endpoint, so the code path exercised in development is the production one. Only the identity provider is replaced, by one that runs locally and starts in about a second.

Availability

Silo is open source and available on GitHub. It can be installed with nix profile add github:hencjo/silo, or run directly from the flake:

nix run github:hencjo/silo -- example-config > config.yaml
nix run github:hencjo/silo -- serve --port 9799 --config-file config.yaml

Issues and feedback are welcome.

entry.title: Service modules, port allocation, and process watching in devenv
entry.summary: Contributions to devenv covering service modules, port allocation, process watching, and evaluation caching.
entry.content:
Background

devenv is a Nix-based tool for declarative, reproducible developer environments, combining languages, packages, services, and processes in a single file. This site is built with it.

Contribution

  • added the services.mosquitto module, with tests and documentation
  • worked on the MongoDB module, including services.mongodb.replication
  • improved RabbitMQ port allocation for distribution and EPMD ports
  • allocated OpenTelemetry Collector listener ports
  • fixed process watching so that processes are not restarted on irrelevant file events
  • tightened dynamic port allocation and evaluation-cache behaviour
  • added regression tests for port allocation across repositories

Discussion

When working across many projects, an environment tool is either unobtrusive or a source of friction. Port collisions between repositories and spurious restarts are typical examples of the latter, and are a common reason for abandoning reproducible environments altogether.

entry.title: Two contributions to Argo, a dependency-free JSON library for Java
entry.summary: A fix for incomplete reads in Argo's position-tracking reader (2016), and buffered reading in its parser (2026).
entry.content:
Background

Argo is a JSON parser and generator for Java without external dependencies, maintained by Mark Slater and originally hosted on SourceForge.

Contribution

Incomplete reads (2016). Reader.read(char[]) may return fewer characters than the buffer holds, in which case the caller is expected to call it again. Argo's PositionTrackingPushbackReader assumed a single call filled the buffer. With readers backed by local data this rarely shows, but with readers backed by a network buffer it caused parse failures. I changed the reader to keep reading until the buffer is full or the input ends, and added a regression test using a reader that deliberately returns input in small pieces. The maintainer merged the fix.

Buffered reading (2026). Pull request #19 changed JsonParser to read from its Reader into a small character buffer instead of one character at a time. This reduces per-character overhead and follows the usual Reader.read(char[]) pattern, without changing parsing behaviour.

Discussion

Both changes concern the same boundary: how a parser consumes its input. The first is a correctness issue that only appears with certain kinds of input source, which is why the regression test simulates one rather than relying on local data. Small libraries without dependencies are a recurring preference in my work, and Argo is one I have used for a long time.

entry.title: An HTTP interface to wkhtmltopdf, in Haskell
entry.summary: A small REST service around wkhtmltopdf: it accepts a URL and returns a PDF.
entry.content:
Background

Generating PDFs from HTML is a common requirement, and wkhtmltopdf performs it well. It is, however, a command-line tool with native dependencies, and having every application invoke it directly spreads those dependencies across systems.

Approach

A small Haskell web service wraps wkhtmltopdf. It accepts a URL and returns the rendered PDF.

Discussion

The service confines an awkward native dependency behind a minimal HTTP interface, so that client applications need only HTTP. It was also an opportunity to apply Haskell to a production-oriented problem.

entry.title: An LDAP authenticator for Summer Security
entry.summary: A companion library that adds LDAP authentication to Summer Security.
entry.content:
Approach

This library provides an LDAP Authenticator for Summer Security, so that the same small, code-configured filter can authenticate users against a corporate directory.

Discussion

It illustrates a consequence of keeping the core small: authentication backends are explicitly wired components, so adding LDAP support amounts to a companion library rather than a configuration exercise.

entry.title: Showing the repository-relative path in a Bash prompt
entry.summary: Small Bash helpers for Git-aware prompts.
entry.content:
Background

In deep, Maven-style directory trees, the \w escape in a Bash prompt expands to a long path, and the relevant part, the position within the repository, is difficult to see.

Approach

__git_relative_subdir replaces \w with the working directory relative to the Git root:

~/demo $ cd git-repo/
 master / $ cd module1/src/main/java/
 master /module1/src/main/java $

It can be combined with __git_ps1 to show the branch and status.

Discussion

The change is small, but a prompt is read many times a day, and it is reasonable for it to show the most relevant information.

entry.title: Database migrations with an explicitly declared order
entry.summary: A small Java database migration library in which migrations and their order are declared in code.
entry.content:
Background

Migration tools of the period typically relied on classpath scanning, naming conventions, XML configuration, and a logging framework. Which migrations ran, and in which order, depended on what was discovered at runtime rather than on what had been specified.

Approach

Migrations are declared explicitly in Java:

migrations(
  migration("1.0-baseline").installsThrough(script("1.0-baseline.sql")),
  migration("1.1-base64-decode-some-field", V1_1_Migrations.base64decodeSomeField())
);

SQL scripts and Java-based migrations can be combined, and further migration types can be added.

Discussion

The design goals are intentionally modest: minimal dependencies, no logging framework, configuration in code, and no resource discovery. A missing script causes the upgrade to fail rather than silently altering it. The library is an early example of a principle that recurs in my later work: important inputs should be explicit.

entry.title: Web authentication as an ordered list of rules in Java
entry.summary: A small, dependency-free Java library that expresses web authentication as a code-first DSL.
entry.content:
Background

Many Java web applications require authentication and little else. The security frameworks available at the time brought XML configuration, implicit global state, and a large surface area relative to what was often a handful of rules.

Approach

Summer Security is a servlet filter configured through a small DSL. Rules are evaluated in order, and the first matching rule determines the response:

summer(logger,
  when(pathBeginsWith("/img/")).thenAllow(),
  when(formBasedLogin.loginRequest()).then(formBasedLogin.performLoginRequest()),
  when(session.exists()).thenAllow(),
  when(httpBasicAuthenticator.authorizes()).thenAllow(),
  otherwise().then(redirect("/login.html"))
);

It supports HTTP Basic and form-based login (compatible with Spring Security conventions), and can be extended through custom request matchers and responders.

Discussion

The complete policy is readable top to bottom in one place. The authenticated user is derived from the request rather than held in thread-local state, the library has no dependencies, and its scope is limited to authentication; authorization is left to the application.

entry.title: Structuring a pull request for review: a jOOQ bug fix
entry.summary: A fix for inserting PostgreSQL string arrays containing quotes or backslashes, later cited by the jOOQ project as an example pull request.
entry.content:
Background

jOOQ is a type-safe SQL DSL and code generator for Java. At the time, inserting values into PostgreSQL string arrays failed when the strings contained " or \ characters.

Contribution

I submitted a pull request correcting the escaping. The change was deliberately ordered as a sequence of small steps: preparatory refactorings first, then a regression test that reproduced the defect, and finally the fix itself.

Discussion

The jOOQ blog later used this pull request as its example in How to provide a good pull request. The fix itself was minor. The observation I took from it is that the order and granularity of a change largely determine how easily it can be reviewed.
